articles.title: Olivier Mourgue obituary
articles.summary: Designer whose flexible furniture for informal 60s living gave a futuristic look to Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey. Olivier Mourgue always wanted to design the future.
body: Mourgue, who has died aged 87, set out to design furniture that belonged to the modern world, and blurred the boundaries between furniture and architecture. In his view, that meant that it should be flexible, informal, affordable and as close to the floor as possible. He succeeded in a way that he could not have expected.

The film director Stanley Kubrick made Mourgue’s designs an essential part of popular culture’s expectations of how the future would look, even though Mourgue’s work was produced by the thousand rather than in millions. Kubrick used a cluster of Mourgue’s Djinn armchairs to equip the lobby of the Hilton hotel orbiting the moon on Space Station V for one of the key scenes of 2001: A Space Odyssey. The Djinn seemed to float almost weightless, like a colourful bubble of air. There were no conventional arms or legs to be seen. Instead there was a lightweight steel structure and some sturdy rubber webbing to support the foam upholstery, all hidden inside a seamless surface.
points: Designer whose flexible furniture for informal 60s living gave a futuristic look to Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey.

articles.title: Getting into the swing of playing golf | Letters
articles.summary: Readers respond to Adrian Chiles’s article on his antipathy to the game. I have some sympathies with Adrian Chiles’s war of attrition with golf ( I hate golf, 14 October ).
body: Over the 60 years that I have been playing, I have learned that it is possible to master some of this game some of the time, but not all of the time. There are many other pluses to this wonderful game. I have played golf on many courses in this country and in Europe, enjoying great views and friendships along the way.

I can readily identify with the myriad frustrations that Adrian Chiles identifies in his experiences of playing golf. However, after more than 50 years of playing without any discernible improvement, I still soldier on o’er hill and dale, wielding my mashie niblick.

I do so because of all the positive benefits to be gained from a four-hour walk unspoiled: the exercise, the beautiful scenery, the fresh air and, as much as anything, the banter and bonhomie with my old schoolmates as we mercilessly mock our collective inability to master the game.

articles.title: ‘Don’t sweat the small stuff’: hospice workers share 12 lessons about life and death
articles.summary: Hospice and end-of-life workers discuss what they’ve learned from their work and patients in their last moments. “Hospice” can be a loaded term. Some see it as synonymous with death and “giving up”, as Courtney, a full-time hospice nurse practitioner in Missouri, puts it.
body: “Hospice is giving someone a gift,” she says of her patients, who have typically received a terminal diagnosis with a timeline of six months or less. “It is giving them the gift of being able to stay at home and eat or not eat whatever they want. It is the gift of comfort.”

Courtney first started working with dying patients when she was an oncology nurse. Patients would come to her from the intensive care unit (ICU) or other areas of the hospital when they had a limited time to live and were on comfort measures only – a medical term for care that focuses on relieving pain and distress rather than prolonging life.
“I fell in love with it,” says Courtney. She loved getting the rooms ready, dimming the lights, and creating a gentle, pleasant atmosphere for the patient and their families to say their goodbyes.

After a brief stint working in the ICU, Courtney began working in hospice care full-time. She says her job has reshaped how she approaches her life both personally and professionally. We spoke to her and other hospice and end-of-life workers about what they’ve learned from their work and their patients.

articles.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: don’t want to get your Big Winter Coat out just yet? Try ‘onion dressing’
articles.summary: It’s time to learn the art of layering – and we’re talking a crew neck with a ballet wrap and blazer, not full-on outdoor explorer. Is layering an art? Probably not in the traditional sense. We are not talking the Bayeux tapestry here.
body: The avant-garde layering term to drop in order to sound like a connoisseur this season is onion dressing. Not the most romantic name, but a clear visual for the most refined form of layering, which is fine layers rather than hefty ones. And instead of the top layer covering all beneath it, each piece should be visible. As if we were slicing through the onion and looking at a cross-section if you will excuse me labouring the allium thing. This is layering with finesse rather than brute force. Hems and collars and cuffs give an outfit depth and texture without adding too much bulk. You want to look intriguing and multi-dimensional, not like Joey in Friends wearing all of Chandler’s clothes.

articles.title: The Eggs Scene in ‘You Can See Everything’ Scrambles Reality
articles.summary: This review contains spoilers for the film You Can See Everything. A version of this post originally appeared in Eater Today, which spotlights the freshest news and stories from across the food world every day. Subscribe now.
body: What happens when you take two unreliable narrators — make that three, if you include Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, whose on-camera persona morphs from protective, naive tech bro to unscrupulous grifter — put them in a jar, and shake them? The result is that the more questions are asked, the further the truth drifts out of reach. It’s like staring at a Magic Eye image, slightly crossing your eyes, desperate to make out the hidden 3D subject but never quite managing to see it. Eventually, you start worrying your eyes might get stuck that way.
The discourse surrounding the film is already abundant, but we’re here to talk about the eggs.

If you’re familiar with the hallmarks of Fielderian programming, you know that Fielder is prone to hyperfixating on seemingly mundane details that later return to completely upend viewers’ expectations. In You Can See Everything, one such detail is observed in an exchange between Holmes and Evans as they make eggs. How much can be gleaned from watching someone make breakfast? A lot, apparently.

articles.title: Teen Vogue and Wattpad Launched Their New Romance Series with Tarot Readings and Zodiac-Inspired Looks
articles.summary: Teen Vogue hosted an astrology-themed bash at downtown bookstore McNally Jackson to celebrate the launch of I Saw The Signs, its original romance fiction series in partnership with Wattpad Books.
body: Earlier that day, the inaugural installment had dropped. The first chapter of the book Under The Northern Stars by Tay Marley is described by Teen Vogue’s creative editorial director Mi-Anne Chan as “a spicy romance between a science-obsessed nerdy girl and her boy-next-door, teen bronco-riding champion neighbor.” The other books, Read To Me by Ariana Godoy and ​​Star-Crossed Rivals by Anna Todd and E.M. Wilson, will debut in early 2027, each using astrology as a lens to explore relationships.

The original fiction project is the first of its kind for Teen Vogue and a “natural next step” according to Chan, given the publication’s past coverage of fanbases within youth culture. Fan fiction also provides a “world building” opportunity and a chance to invite audiences to find their niche. This is part of Wattpad’s draw for young creatives, too—its self-publishing and community format encourages judgment-free expression and imagination. “You can explore a lot of different themes through a familiar world and familiar stories. It’s the way that writers develop their voice, in the way that they explore things through different universes,” Chan explained.

articles.title: The United States Just Got a New National Park For the First Time in Six Years
articles.summary: Located in the southeastern corner of Arizona, this 12,000-acre park is known for its unique rock formations, pristine stargazing, and scenic canyon drives.
body: The US national park list is growing for the first time in nearly six years. Chiricahua National Monument, located in southeastern Arizona, was officially designated as the 64th national park in the US on October 20, 2026 following President Trump's signature on the Chiricahua National Park Act.

The new park lies just over an hour from the Arizona–New Mexico border and is nicknamed the “Wonderland of Rocks” for its towering rock spires and unusual formations, the result of a volcanic eruption about 27 million years ago.

Chiricahua was originally established as a national monument in 1924, and today boasts more than 17 miles of hiking trails for exploring on foot, as well as the Bonita Canyon Scenic Drive, a picturesque road that winds through rock formations.

For outdoors lovers, the designation is big news. The last US landmark to receive a new national park designation was West Virginia’s New River Gorge National Park & Preserve in 2020, home to one of the oldest rivers in the world and the deepest and longest river gorge in the Appalachians.

articles.title: After Years of Hard Water Damage, I Finally Found the Right Shampoo
articles.summary: Shampoos for hard water will help keep your hair feeling hydrated and healthy overall. Here, the experts break down everything you need to know about hard water and which shampoos you should try to keep hair looking and feeling healthy.
body: One of the few downsides of growing up in Los Angeles is dealing with the city’s very hard water. Thanks to the mineral buildup, my teenage and college years were spent trying different hair products to make my thick, long hair feel less dry (and oh, it was dry) and look less dull. It all changed when I learned the key to washing hair in hard water is in my shampoo.

As Morgan Rabach, MD, board-certified dermatologist at LM Medical NYC, explains, certain shampoos, also known as chelating shampoos, are designed specifically to bind to minerals so that they can be rinsed away easily. When incorporating it into your routine, a shampoo for hard water sets up a good base for your hair to stay healthy and mineral-free.

“The biggest thing is preventing mineral buildup,” says Corinne Erickson, MD, board-certified dermatologist and founder of Georgia Skin Specialists. “Hard water contains minerals like calcium and magnesium that can accumulate on your hair, leaving it feeling dry, dull, stiff, and harder to manage.”
So if you’re dealing with hard water and looking for a shampoo to help revive your hair from all that debris and buildup, consider these seven recs below.

articles.summary: We may earn a commission from links on this page. Deal pricing and availability subject to change after time of publication. An ultra-wide curved gaming monitor with ridiculous specs is every gamer's dream, but they (usually) don't come cheap.
body: The Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 Series is not a regular ultra-wide gaming monitor. It has impressive specs, but you'll need a top-notch gaming computer with specific outputs to take full advantage of its 240Hz refresh rate potential.

This monitor came out in 2023 with an "excellent" review from PCMag, mainly due to its impressive 7,680 by 2,160 4K native resolution, the ridiculous 57-inch screen size, its great color range and accuracy, the 240Hz refresh rate, and its design. The VA panel also means you get a bright 1,000-nit screen. To make full use of its powerful 240Hz refresh rate, you'll need to use a DisplayPort 2.1, or you'll be limited to 120Hz. You'll also need a powerful modern graphics card that is able to push the frames at a native resolution to max out the monitor's potential.

Although it is pricey, this monitor is a great value for the right gamer. You'll need plenty of space to fit a 57-inch screen, as well as a powerful computer to justify using the monitor—if you're not a competitive gamer with a powerful computer, it's probably not worth the price tag. Instead, consider this Asus gaming monitor going for $329.99 (originally $499) right now.
